title: How to wash fruits and vegetables correctly

seo.title: How to wash fruits and vegetables safely
seo.meta_description: Use potable running water, friction, clean hands and tools, and drying. Rinse produce even before peeling, and do not use dish soap on food.
seo.search_intent: Learn the correct household method for washing fruits and vegetables and avoid practices that can recontaminate produce.

excerpt: Rinse fruits and vegetables under potable running water while rubbing the surface, and use a clean brush on firm produce. Wash even before peeling. Washing reduces microbes but does not sterilize food, and dish soap should not be used on produce.
content_html:
Washing fruits and vegetables does not require a special product or elaborate routine. For home use, the core steps are simple: clean hands, potable running water, friction on the surface, and avoiding recontamination afterward. Washing reduces dirt and microbes, but it does not sterilize produce.

Wash produce even when you plan to peel it

The FDA recommends rinsing all produce under running water before preparation or eating, including produce with skins and rinds you will not consume. Washing first reduces the chance that a knife carries contamination from the outside into the edible flesh.

Start with clean hands and use a clean counter, knife, and cutting board, particularly if raw meat, poultry, seafood, or eggs have been handled nearby.

Running water and friction do the basic work

Hold produce under potable running water and rub the surface with your hands. For firm items such as melons and cucumbers, FDA guidance recommends using a clean produce brush.

Hot water is not necessary. Extreme water temperature is not a reliable home sanitizing method and can damage some produce.

Leafy vegetables need access between the leaves

For lettuce, chard, and other leafy vegetables, remove damaged or heavily soiled portions and separate leaves so water can reach the surfaces. Drain them well afterward. Gentle handling with fresh water is more useful than leaving produce indefinitely in the same bowl of water.

If a package is labeled pre-washed or ready-to-eat, follow the package directions. Rewashing in a contaminated sink or with unclean utensils can introduce microbes again.

Drying is useful too

The FDA suggests drying produce with a clean cloth or paper towel after washing. This can remove additional surface material and also improves texture and storage when excess moisture would otherwise remain.

Washing reduces risk; it does not make risk zero

FDA guidance is explicit that washing can reduce bacteria on fresh produce but will not eliminate all of it. Refrigeration, discarding rotten produce, preventing cross-contamination, and cooking when appropriate still matter.

People at higher risk of serious foodborne illness may need to follow additional guidance about certain raw foods.

Do not use dish soap or hand soap on produce

Soaps and detergents are designed for dishes or hands, not to remain on porous foods. The FDA does not recommend washing fruits and vegetables with soap, detergent, or commercial produce washes whose residue safety and effectiveness have not been established for routine household use.

A simple sequence to remember

Wash your hands; cut away damaged areas; rinse under running water; rub or brush firm surfaces; dry with something clean; and keep the washed produce away from utensils that touched raw animal foods.

That does not make a lettuce leaf sterile, but it reduces contamination in a practical way without adding unnecessary chemicals.

faq.question: Do you need to wash fruit if you will peel it?
faq.answer: Yes. Washing first reduces the chance that a knife transfers surface contamination into the flesh.

faq.question: Should vegetables be washed with soap?
faq.answer: No. For routine household washing, use potable running water and friction rather than dish or hand soap.

faq.question: Does washing remove all bacteria?
faq.answer: No. It can reduce surface contamination but does not sterilize produce.
